Five great drums of hay sit in a loose uneven scatter on the pale bristled cut floor, each throwing a long shadow raking across it from one side. The twine on the nearest has gone furry and pale.
Eight enormous cylinders of packed hay sit spread wide and uneven across the cut floor, no two at the same angle. One has drifted a full pace clear of the rest and sits entirely alone.

Six great drums rest scattered across the pale bristled floor, their cut ends all facing different directions, each a tight spiral of pale stalks. A sparrow works the floor right behind the outermost one.
Seven bales sit in a loose spread, the far three half-obscured by hay dust still up in the air above the cut floor. The nearest one has a single long loose strand of hay dangling from its twine.

Four enormous cylinders sit spread wide on the cut floor, each throwing its long shadow raking across the bristled ground from one side. A hare sits up small beside the outermost, entirely unbothered.
Nine great drums of hay sit unevenly scattered across the pale cut floor, the gaps between them wide and irregular. The twine on three of them has gone the same bleached colour as the hay beneath it.

Six bales sit in a loose uneven spread, one rolled a clear half-pace out from the others and sitting at a slight tilt. Hay dust is still up in the air above the cut floor between them, every mote of it lit.

Eight great cylinders rest scattered wide across the cut floor, their cut ends a repeating pattern of tight-packed spirals. A small dog lies flat out and fully committed in the one patch of shade beneath the nearest.

Six bales built up two and three deep against the field gate, the stack a little out of true and leaning left at the top. The twine on the highest one has gone pale and furry, loose ends lifting in the air.

Eight great drums stacked against the hedge two deep and four wide, one set slightly out of true and resting against its neighbour. A linen jacket has been thrown over the top bar of the gate beside them.

Seven bales stacked against the stone wall, three on the bottom, two on the next, two more on top and leaning a little. The twine on the topmost has frayed and gone as pale as old rope left in the yard.

Six great drums built against the field gate two deep, the top layer sitting well back from the edge and one tipped a fraction off its axis. A wooden hay rake leans against the gate post beside the stack.

A wooden flat-bed wagon piled far too high with loose hay leans and overhangs its own plank sides, hay slithering slowly off the back end. A wooden rake lies flat across the top of the load to hold it down.

A wooden flat-bed wagon heaped with loose hay stands with the load bulging out past its own sides on both ends. A cat sits at the very peak of the heap, composed and entirely self-satisfied, not holding on.
A wooden wagon loaded to an almost architectural height with loose hay leans a little to one side on uneven ground. A coiled rope and a wooden rake lie across the plank bench at the front.

A wooden flat-bed wagon piled well past sensible with loose hay has a great slow avalanche of it sliding off the left side as it stands. A two-pronged pitchfork is jammed upright into the top of the load at a determined angle.

A long combed ridge of raked dry grass lies across the pale cut floor, open and airy, ready to be gathered. A single long feather, pheasant-barred, has come down and rests across the top of the ridge.

A soft heap of loose hay tumbled from a load sits on the pale bristled floor, a two-pronged pitchfork stood upright in it at a slight lean. The heap is still exhaling a thin drift of hay dust into the still air above it.
A long combed ridge of dry pale-green hay lies across the cut floor, the raked ends all combed one way. Three sparrows work along it from one end, unhurried, pulling seeds loose from the open stems.

One great drum of hay sits square in the hedge at the foot of the slope where it rolled, the flattened pale track it pressed still showing behind it. Eight more sit scattered wide and uneven on the cut floor beyond.

One enormous cylinder of packed hay has come to rest half inside the hedge at the field edge, twine intact, entirely at peace with itself. The bent gap it forced through the hawthorn is still sprung open wide.

One great drum has tipped onto its flat end and stands upright on the cut floor like a drum on a stage, entirely out of place among the seven lying on their sides around it. It has plainly been left exactly like that.

A chipped stone jar of water sits wedged into the shade beneath one of the five great drums scattered on the cut floor. The jar has a cloth stopper and a fern leaf tucked under the twine around its neck.

Two boots and two socks have been set over the twine on one of the six great drums scattered on the cut floor, the socks pushed down into the boots to keep them from blowing. The boots are pointed skyward.

A hollowed gap between two bales in the stack against the gate has been worn smooth from being sat in. A tin cup turned upside-down on the gate post and a hank of twine on a nail are the only other things left.
